newsitem.title: USA: Albright sees two-year window for Cyprus peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees two-year window for Cyprus peace bid.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday that the next two years presented a window of opportunity to tackle the Cyprus crisis despite a recent increase of tension on the divided island.
In an interview with Reuters, Albright admitted she had developed no strategy so far for resolving the Cyprus problem but saw a need to "use the advantage of the calendar."

Albright, who took over as secretary of state on Jan. 23, has signalled several times in testimony before Congress that Cyprus, divided since 1974 between its Greek and Turkish communities, will be one of her priorities.
But some U.S. officials say that with relations at a low ebb between the rival communities, this is not the time for a Cyprus initiative.
"Obviously we're all concerned about the increase in tensions in the island of Cyprus and I think we want to make sure that the situation does not worsen in any way," Albright said.
"But I do think also that ... the 1997-1998 period is a very important one in terms of (Cyprus') desire to accede to the (European Union) and their elections in '98."

Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke spoke more than a year ago of launching a Cyprus peace bid, only to be defeated by a flare-up of tension between Greece and Turkey in the Aegean.

More recently, four people have been killed in shooting incidents along the demarcation line in Cyprus. And an announcement by the Greek Cypriot government that it plans to buy anti-aircraft missiles from Russia drew threats of military strikes from Ankara.
Albright said she did "not have a piece of paper with a strategy on it yet."
"But I do know that it's very important to defuse the tensions and try to use this period as a way that can help us use the advantage of the calendar," she said.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkish troops landed in the north of the Mediterranean island in 1974 in response to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece.
The United Nations has since been trying to reunite Cyprus under a federal system. But the bitter hostility between the two communities has thwarted a series of mediators.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Thursday the world body hoped to continue proximity talks with community leaders in the hope that "we can see enough progress and identify enough common ground for us eventually to have face-to-face talks."

"It would be preferable that the talks take place this year and ideally before September. Otherwise we are going to get into the election fever," he said, referring to elections due to be held by the Greek Cypriots early in 1998.
